newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Jan 13.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Jan 13.

text.p: Damage from Cyclone Drena would be counted in the millions of dollars, Thames Mayor Alasdair Thompson said on Sunday. Homes were flooded when the sea, whipped up by high winds, swept into Thames at high tide on Saturday night. Cyclone Drena was last night off the coast of the South Island. Weekend rain pushed river levels dangerously high and caused slips, flooding problems and road closures in Otago and Southland. Page 1.

Conservation Minister Nick Smith on Sunday criticised his department for taking controversial action without telling him first. The Conservation Department decided to stop retrieving bodies from Mt Cook National Park at Christmas and will stop taking part in search and rescue operations from June. Smith said on Sunday that he found out about the department's decisions only when he read newspaper reports. Page 2.

Reports that tourists had called off trips to New Zealand because they wre unable to get seats on flights have prompted Tourism Minister Murray McCully to order an inquiry. The managing director of Dunedin's Pacific Park hotel, Clarke Walker, said last week that he had several cancellations from prospective visitors who could not get to New Zealand. McCully has asked the Tourism Board to prepare an urgent report. Page 2.

Making the Coalition Government's work-for-the-dole scheme acceptable was discussed at the Green Party's annual policy conference at the weekend, Green Party co-leader Janette Fitzsimons said on Sunday. The party -- one of five constituent members of the Alliance -- met at a Conservation Department lodge in the Kaimai Ranges. Fitzsimons said the party did not support the work-for-the-dole scheme "as it stands", but there were ways it could be made into something positive. Page 2.

Dropping the mandatory life sentence for battered women who killed their partners was unnecessary and against the principles of the New Zealand justice system, sociologist Greg Newbold said on Sunday. Justice Minister Doug Graham said on Friday mandatory life sentences were inappropriate for battered women who murder their partners. Anyone convicted of murder receives a life sentence, of which they must serve at least 10 years before applying for parole, but the government in its coalition agreement is to investigate dropping the mandatory sentence for battered women. Page 2.

In line with its policy to rid the public health system of its profit motive, the government should tell all Crown Health Enterprises not to go ahead with any privatisation plans and options, the Association of Salaried Medical Specialists said on Sunday. Association executive director Ian Powell said some CHEs were considering privatisation options such as contracting out services and joint commercial ventures. Powell said CHEs had resorted to these options because of inadequate government funding but the government intended to boost public health system funding and remove the profit motive. Page 3.

A national survey of Australian business has found a gloomy view of the economy and falling confidence. The December 1996 Survey of Investor Confidence by the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry found that, while expectations of future conditions remained higher than during 1995, confidence had fallen since a high point after the 1996 federal election. Page 13.
